{{Short description|American physical chemist (1920–1985)}}

'''Jerry Donohue''' (June 12, 1920 – February 13, 1985) was an American theoretical and physical chemist.  He is best remembered for steering [[James D. Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]] towards the correct structure of [[DNA]] with some crucial information.

==Early career==
Donohue was born in [[Sheboygan, Wisconsin]] and studied for his first two degrees at [[Dartmouth College]], where he earned his [[Bachelor's degree|A.B.]] in 1941 and his [[Master's degree|M.A.]] in 1943. He worked on his [[Doctorate|PhD]] under [[Linus Pauling]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech), earning his doctorate in 1947.  Donohue remained at Caltech until 1952.<ref name="bio">{{cite web
| url = http://www.archives.upenn.edu/faids/upt/upt50/donohuej.html
| title = Biography
| accessdate = 2006-10-31
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120717071121/http://www.archives.upenn.edu/faids/upt/upt50/donohuej.html
| archive-date = 2012-07-17
| url-status = dead
}}</ref>

==Role in determining structure of deoxyribonucleic acid==
Throughout his life Donohue specialized in crystal structures and analysis, specifically of molecules relating to biology and [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen-bonding]].  In 1952, Donohue was given a Guggenheim Foundation grant<ref>[http://www.gf.org/52fellow.html John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation, Fellowships to Assist Research and Artistic Creation, 1952 U.S. and Canadian Fellows] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050721080429/http://www.gf.org/52fellow.html|date=2005-07-21}}</ref> to study at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]] for 6 months.  He shared an office with Francis Crick and James D. Watson.  In his work to determine the structure of DNA, Watson had been using structure for [[guanine]] from a monograph by [[Norman Davidson (biochemist)|James N. Davidson]].  Davidson had depicted these bases in the [[enol]] configuration and Watson used this structure in an unsuccessful 'like-with-like' pairing of the bases.  Donohue informed Watson that the published structure was just a guess and that the [[Ketone|keto]] structure was more likely, based on a publication of June Broomhead and quantum mechanical calculations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Watson |first=James |title=The Double Helix |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson (London) |year=1968 |isbn=0-582-45181-7}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Judson |first=Horace Freeland |title=The Eighth Day of Creation |publisher=Touchstone (New York) |year=1979 |isbn=0-87969-478-5}}</ref> Within a few days, Watson and Crick were able to build their famous model for DNA.<ref name="bio2">{{cite web |title=Biography |url=http://www.archives.upenn.edu/faids/upt/upt50/donohuej.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120717071121/http://www.archives.upenn.edu/faids/upt/upt50/donohuej.html |archive-date=2012-07-17 |accessdate=2006-10-31}}</ref>

In their famous article by Watson and Crick in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' that proposed the structure of DNA, the following acknowledgment to Donohue appears: "We are much indebted to Dr. Jerry Donohue for constant advice and criticism, especially on interatomic distances".<ref>{{cite journal |last=Watson |first=JD & |author2=Crick, FHC |year=1953 |title=Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid |journal=Nature |volume=171 |issue=4356 |pages=737–738 |bibcode=1953Natur.171..737W |doi=10.1038/171737a0 |pmid=13054692 |s2cid=4253007}}</ref>

==Later life==
After Cambridge, Donohue became Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Southern California]] (USC) where he continued to specialize in hydrogen-bonding.  He also studied sulfur-containing compounds and began to publish papers more extensively on crystallography and crystal structures.  From 1963-1966, he was chairman of the USC Chemistry Department.

In 1966, Donohue joined the chemistry faculty of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] (Penn) as the Rhodes-Thompson Professor of Chemistry.  In 1974, he published his book ''The Structures of the Elements''.  He retired from his Penn position because of ill-health in 1985, and died that same year from cancer.<ref name="bio" /><ref>{{cite journal | title=Crystallographers | journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography | volume=18 | issue=3 | pages=188–189 | year=1985 | doi=10.1107/S002188988501010X| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Ladd | first=Mark, and Sidney Kettle | title=In memoriam: Professor Jerry Donohue | journal=Journal of Chemical Crystallography | volume=15 | issue=4 | pages=303 | date=August 1985 | doi=10.1007/BF01160723 | s2cid=95125217 }}</ref>

Donohue was married to Patricia Schreier.  They had a son and a daughter.  His leisure-time interests included sea shells<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://s190418054.onlinehome.us/HSN/1970/7407.pdf |last=Donohue |first=Jerry |title=Three Novel Cones from New Caledonia |journal=Hawaiian Shell News |volume=22 |issue=7 |pages=3 |date=July 1974 |accessdate=2009-05-14 }}{{dead link|date=April 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and horticulture.
